g.text: FM0/FM1 bi-phase - the receiver, which is the whole act
STATUS: designed WIP, on fw-timing-protocols, not in main, 7/7 checks RED
RECEIVER - the half that is the act
RELEASED
PINOE = 0x00 - RELEASE EVERY PAD, AND IN
PARTICULAR THE INPUT.
THIS IS THE WHOLE DECODER IN ONE BIT.
A pad
the firmware DRIVES reads back its own register
through PIN, not the wire, so claiming the input
pad means the firmware never sees the stream at
all.
The first version CLAIMED the input - writing
BMC_IN to PINOE, reasoning that "the input is the
device's, so claim it" - and the symptom was that
NO TRANSITION WAS EVER DETECTED
, which reads
as a decoder that does not work rather than as an
enable written backwards.
It is the SIXTH time in this block that a level and
an enable have been confused, and the only reason
it was found at all is that the testbench's check
NAMES THE FLAG and the flag was 0xFF.
see the bounce note for the ISA constraint here
SAMPLE
timestamp the level
IN A, PIN; AND A, BMC_IN
now = the 1 us counter
A BI-PHASE RECEIVER DOES NOT SYNCHRONISE ON A LEVEL.
It TIMESTAMPS the level and compares it with the
level recorded at the last CHANGE - and it is that
comparison which recovers the clock. There is no
other clock in the system.
CHANGED?
dmem[4] = the level at the last CHANGE
dmem[5] = its microsecond timestamp
THE BOUNCE, AND IT IS FORCED BY THE ISA.
On this machine the store-forward a transition
detector wants cannot be written: OP_LDS (0xB) is
a <= ram[x] with NO X destination, so X = ram[X]
is inexpressible, and the encoding that looks like
it, LDM X,addr with arg[7]=1, is a DIRECT load whose
address field is the top NIBBLE only and cannot even
name byte 8. So the old level lives in a MEMORY
byte.
And that byte belongs to this decoder and to NOTHING
ELSE: a scratch shared between a routine and its
caller is how the DS18B20 act lost a byte counter to
the delay routine.
FOLD
intervals into BITS
dmem[8] += 1 per half-interval, and the bit
is decided ONCE PER BIT rather than once per
transition, because a bit is TWO half-intervals and
A DATA TRANSITION INSIDE A BIT IS WHAT DISTINGUISHES
FM0 FROM FM1.
This is the design decision the act exists to make.
A sample-based edge detector cannot distinguish the
two encodings at all.
FLAG
which encoding
dmem[3]: 0 = FM0, 1 = FM1, 0xFF = no transitions
A RUN OF ONES IN FM1 IS A CLEAN SQUARE WAVE
one transition per bit, in the middle - and the
decoder recovers its clock from exactly those
transitions.
IT IS NOT A DECODABLE-NOTHING CASE
the first version of the TB claimed it was, and the
claim was in the TB header, in the encoder, and in
two WORKLOG lines, and was wrong in all four.
BANK
the three bytes
dmem[0..2], LSB first, from the wire rules
rather than from the firmware
STATUS
7 of 7 checks RED
e708e69 the RED TB
b2cb76c the first
firmware draft, which
ASSEMBLES and RUNS
the act is no longer RED because there
is no firmware - it is RED because a first
draft does not yet decode.
THE DISTINCTION MATTERS: the checks are the
REFERENCE now, not a description of them.
TRANSMITTER - the smaller half
DECODE -> ENCODE
dmem[11]
after the three bytes are recovered, the same
program ENCODES a byte on the OTHER pad, and
NEITHER SIDE IS TOLD WHAT THE OTHER SENT
COUNT
the half-interval
120 clocks =
2 us
, and it is COUNTED, not
waited on: the receiver timestamps in whole
microseconds, and a period that is not a whole
number of them would make this act's OWN arithmetic
the least accurate thing in it.
THE BIT PERIOD IS A WHOLE NUMBER OF MICROSECONDS
BECAUSE THE COMPARISON IS ONLY EXACT THEN.
SHIFT
the byte out
dmem[6] the byte, dmem[7] the bit counter,
dmem[12,13] the bit under construction and then
the byte being shifted out
TESTBENCH - two decoders, written from the WIRE RULES
ENCB
encodes a byte on IN_PAD, and the firmware
must recover it
DECODE
the firmware's output
decodes the firmware's stream on OUT_PAD
WRITTEN FROM THE SAME WIRE RULES, NOT FROM THE
FIRMWARE
and the act was written with TWO decoders for exactly
that reason - one decoder and one encoder that
agree by construction would agree even when both are
wrong, and the first version of this file was the TB
header, the encoder and two WORKLOG lines all
asserting the same false claim about a run of ones.
WHY THIS ACT IS NOT A SEVENTH TIMING ACT.
Every other act in this block is judged on a WAVEFORM a receiver can decode. This
one is judged on a
RECEIVER
: the code lives in the TRANSITIONS, not in the
levels, and the only clock in the system is the one the receiver recovers from the
data.
So the claim is not "the firmware drives a bi-phase stream" but
"the firmware
RECOVERS THE CLOCK from a stream it shares no clock with, and says which encoding it
locked onto."
CONSEQUENCE ONE: A HELD-CONSTANT LINE IS NOT A FRAME, AND
THE FIRMWARE'S ANSWER MUST BE A DECLARED FAILURE.
EVERY bit of a well-formed frame carries a transition in its middle, because
"bi-phase" means the level changes WITHIN the interval. So a line held CONSTANT -
which is what a disconnected, shorted or dead sensor looks like on the wire - has
no transitions at all and carries no clock, and a receiver that locked on to it
has locked on to nothing.
THAT is the stream the last check presents, and the firmware's answer to it must
be a
DECLARED FAILURE rather than a byte it invented:
a decoder that cannot
fail is not a decoder.
THE LIMITS, stated rather than buried.
Three bytes per direction,
because the machine has SIXTEEN BYTES of data
memory and a receiver's state - the transition timestamp, the previous level, the
bit counter, the phase flag and the frame being assembled - is most of that, and a
scratch byte for the store-forward the ISA cannot express is most of the rest.
One inter-frame gap, and no noise, no jitter and no line-length limit.
Those
are the things a real receiver's worst case lives in, and pretending otherwise
would be claiming a robustness this act does not test.
no change: keep timestamping
the level moved
two half-intervals: the bit is decided
a byte is complete
